item.title: Five Breakthroughs and a Dishwasher
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
The Jetsons went on air in September 1962 and, as Max Bennett points out at the start of A Brief History of Intelligence, got a surprising amount of the future right: video calls, flat screens, cell phones, 3D printing, smartwatches. What it did not get right was the one thing it took for granted, Rosey, the robot who kept the house, helped with homework, and noticed when the family was about to quarrel. Sixty years later we still have nothing like her. “It is no secret that the first company to build a robot that can simply load a dishwasher will immediately have a bestselling product,” Bennett writes. “All attempts to do this have failed. It isn’t fundamentally a mechanical problem; it’s an intellectual one.”

That is the question the book sets out to answer: why can a machine beat anyone alive at chess, yet not load a dishwasher as well as a six-year-old? It is also the question I brought to it. I spend my working days building systems around language models, and I wanted a better account of what those models do not have. Bennett is not a neuroscientist, which I count in his favour. “I wrote this book because I wanted to read this book,” he says in the introduction; it grew out of reading, long email exchanges with researchers, and a few papers of his own.

I give it 7.5 out of 10. The premise is one of the best I have met in a book about AI, and the book has more depth than I was ready for. It was also slow to read, and I will come back to why.

Five breakthroughs

Bennett’s argument is that intelligence was not built in one piece. It came in five steps, each one resting on the steps before it, and each step solved a problem that the older machinery could not. He tells it as an evolutionary story, from worm-like animals to fish to the first mammals, primates, and humans. For each step he finds the idea in AI that does the same job, and that pairing is what makes the book worth reading for anyone who builds software.

BreakthroughWhat it addsIts counterpart in AI
SteeringSorting the world into good and bad, and turning toward the one and away from the otherThe first Roomba, with a handful of sensors and two choices: go forward or turn
ReinforcingRepeating what led to good outcomes; dopamine as a signal of a prediction that was wrongTemporal difference learning, actor and critic, TD-Gammon
SimulatingAn inner model of the world, so an animal can try things in imagination before it tries them in the worldModel-based reinforcement learning, AlphaZero searching future moves
MentalizingA model of one’s own mind, and through it the minds of others: intent, imitation, planning for needs one does not have yetImitation and inverse reinforcement learning, a helicopter that learns to fly from a pilot’s demonstrations
SpeakingNames and grammar that tie inner simulations together, so ideas outlive the person who had themLarge language models

Each part of the book ends with a summary of its breakthrough, and reading the five summaries in a row is the fastest way to see the whole argument. The thread that runs through them is learning: first by reflex, then by trial and error, then by imagination, then by watching others, then by being told.

Steering: good and bad

The first part starts with the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, a worm with 302 neurons, which Bennett uses as a stand-in for the first animals with a brain. A worm cannot see where food is. It can only tell whether the smell is getting stronger or weaker, and turn. Its sensory neurons report straight away whether a thing is good or bad, which psychologists call valence. “Valence isn’t about a moral judgment,” Bennett writes; “it’s something far more primitive: whether an animal will respond to a stimulus by approaching it or avoiding it.”

The AI parallel is the first Roomba, which Rodney Brooks’s company iRobot sold in 2002. It had a handful of sensors and could only go forward or turn, and it cleaned a whole flat without a map. The detail I liked best is Dirt Detect: when a Roomba finds a patch of dirt, it starts turning in circles, and keeps doing so for a while after the dirt is gone, because dirt in one spot predicts dirt nearby. That, Bennett argues, is what an affective state is for. A worm that smells food stays in a state of searching after the smell has faded; a worm that has eaten settles into a state of rest. In the nematode, dopamine marks “the something-good-is-nearby chemical” and serotonin “the something-good-is-actually-happening chemical.”

Chapter 3 carries this into humans with one of the more unsettling experiments in the book. In the 1960s the psychiatrist Robert Heath gave patients a button that stimulated their own dopamine neurons, and they pressed it, sometimes hundreds of times an hour, not because it felt good but because it never quite did. “Dopamine is not a signal for pleasure itself,” Bennett concludes; “it is a signal for the anticipation of future pleasure.” It is hard to read that today without thinking of the feeds on our phones.

Chapter 4 closes the part with learning, and with a problem every machine learning engineer knows: credit assignment. If you tap a slug and shock it, how does it know to link the shock to the tap, and not to the temperature of the water or the texture of the ground? Bennett lists four tricks the earliest brains use, which Pavlov had already found in his dogs: eligibility traces, overshadowing, latent inhibition, and blocking. Blocking is the one that stayed with me. “Once an animal has established an association between a predictive cue and a response, all further cues that overlap with the predictive cue are blocked from association with that response.” It is a crude rule and a sensible one, and it is also the kind of inertia I see in agents whose memory has settled on an early explanation and no longer lets a better one in.

Reinforcing: learning from what was not expected

In the second part, the biology and the computer science meet in one story. In 1984 Richard Sutton finished a dissertation that proposed temporal difference learning: instead of waiting for the end of a game to learn whether a move was good, a system learns from the change in its own prediction from one moment to the next. Sutton had studied psychology, not computer science, and Bennett makes a point of it: “He didn’t want to understand the best way to tackle the temporal credit assignment problem; he wanted to understand the actual way that animals solved it.” In 1994 Gerald Tesauro’s TD-Gammon, which learned backgammon purely by playing itself, reached what Tesauro called a “truly staggering level of performance.”

Then the neuroscientist Wolfram Schultz recorded dopamine neurons in monkeys that had learned to expect sugar water after a picture. When the reward came unexpectedly, dopamine went up. When the picture appeared and the sugar did not, dopamine dropped, even though the surprise was the same. Once the researchers working on temporal difference learning saw his data, “they immediately knew what they were seeing. The dopamine responses that Schultz found in monkeys aligned exactly with Sutton’s temporal difference learning signal.” Bennett’s one-line summary corrects the popular picture of dopamine twice over: “Dopamine is not a signal for reward but for reinforcement.”

Chapter 8, “Why Life Got Curious”, adds the missing ingredient. Reinforcement learning systems that had mastered Atari games could not get through the first level of Montezuma’s Revenge, a game where the reward comes only after a long walk through rooms full of traps. “It wasn’t until 2018 when an algorithm was developed that finally completed level one,” and what it added was curiosity, a reward for seeing something new. Bennett finds the same thing in fish, mice, monkeys, and infants (“surprise itself triggers the release of dopamine, even if there is no ‘real’ reward”) and uses it to explain gambling, which violates every simple theory of learning from reward. I had read about Montezuma’s Revenge before; I had not seen it set beside a slot machine.

Smell, the first pattern

Chapter 7, “The Problems of Pattern Recognition”, is where the book clicked for me, because Bennett explains neural networks with the nose. A smell is not one molecule but a mixture that lights up a pattern across many kinds of olfactory neurons, and the first vertebrates were the first animals that could read such patterns. From there he walks through the two problems any pattern recogniser has to solve, discrimination and generalisation, shows how the early cortex may solve them with expansion, sparsity, and auto-association, and then shows how an artificial network solves them with backpropagation, the method Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart and Ronald Williams popularised in the 1980s. His running example for the machine is a network that learns to tell egg smells from flower smells. Hinton, who returns in chapter 11 with the Helmholtz machine, is also one of the central figures of Empire of AI.

The chapter then moves on to catastrophic forgetting (a network taught to add twos forgets how to add ones, in McCloskey and Cohen’s 1989 experiment) and to the invariance problem in vision, where Hubel and Wiesel’s cats lead to Fukushima’s convolutional networks. Smell is the quiet hinge here: an egg smells the same from any angle, so smell has no invariance problem, and it is the one sense that bypasses the thalamus.

I wrote more about this, and about why I think smell will be the last sense we learn to read and write with machines, in a note: Smell is pattern recognition.

Simulating: imagining before doing

The third part is the one I keep thinking about at work. Its subject is the neocortex, which Bennett treats as a single repeated circuit. Vernon Mountcastle found in the mid-twentieth century that neurons in one vertical column of the cortex respond alike, and the idea that every column runs the same algorithm leads Bennett to Hermann von Helmholtz, who suggested in the nineteenth century that we do not perceive the world directly but perceive “what the brain thinks is there,” a process he called inference. Geoffrey Hinton and Peter Dayan built a proof of concept in 1995 and called it the Helmholtz machine. If perception is the cortex generating a world and checking it against the senses, then some neuroscientists are right to call it, as Bennett quotes, a “constrained hallucination.” Cut off the senses and the hallucination runs free.

I find that a useful way to think about language models. A model answering from its weights alone is a generative model without senses, and what we call hallucination is the free-running case. Tools and retrieval are the constraint: they play the part the eyes play for the cortex. That is my reading, not Bennett’s, but it fits what I see in practice. Bennett also suggests that dreaming may keep the generative model stable, “a process of forced generation” to balance a day of recognition, which is close to an idea I wrote down about agent memory that dreams.

In the 1930s Edward Tolman, at Berkeley, noticed that rats at a hard fork in a maze would stop and look left and right for a few seconds before choosing. Tolman guessed the rat was “playing out” each option first, and called it “vicarious trial and error.” The idea fell out of favour for lack of evidence, until recordings in the 2000s let researchers watch a rat’s neurons while it paused and see it sweep through the paths ahead. “Tolman was right,” Bennett writes: the rats were planning. Other experiments in chapter 12 show rats that pass up a mediocre treat for a better one, find that the better one comes with a long wait, and look back at the door they gave up, which is what regret looks like from the outside. Even memory turns out to be simulation: “we don’t truly remember episodic events. The process of episodic remembering is one of simulating an approximate re-creation of the past.”

Chapter 13 gives the machine version. Temporal difference learning was enough for backgammon, but not for Go, and what AlphaZero added in 2017 was the rat’s pause: it simulated future moves before it made one. That is the same split I wrote about in Plan, then let go: an agent that drafts the whole plan before it acts behaves very differently from one that reacts step by step, and the draft is the agent’s version of the rat’s pause at the fork. Bennett also shows the other side. In the 1980s Tony Dickinson trained rats to press a lever for food, then made the food make them ill. Rats that had pressed the lever a few times stopped; rats that had pressed it five hundred times kept going. “Dickinson had discovered habits.” Planning and habit are the same duality Kahneman calls slow and fast thinking, and Bennett is careful to say that “Neither is better; each has its benefits and costs.” That is the argument I made about agents and workflows in Determinism is what intelligence leaves behind: a path explored often enough becomes a habit worth keeping, and the skill is in knowing when to plan and when to repeat.

The hard part of planning is choosing what to simulate, since no brain can play out every future. Bennett’s proposal is that the oldest part of the frontal cortex builds a model of the animal itself and constructs “intent” to explain its own behaviour, and that intent is what narrows the search. He is open that this is a hypothesis. Chapter 14 then answers the question from the introduction, as far as anyone can: “The secret to dishwashing robots lives somewhere in the motor cortex and the broader motor system of mammals.” We do not yet understand how the motor cortex plans fine movements so flexibly, or how it keeps learning as it goes. I liked that the part ends on an open problem rather than a solution.

Mentalizing: a model of one’s own mind

The fourth breakthrough is the one Bennett calls, in some ways, the hardest to reverse engineer in AI. It starts with politics among monkeys. In the 1980s and 1990s Nicholas Humphrey, Frans de Waal, and Robin Dunbar argued that primate brains grew to handle society rather than the jungle, and Dunbar found that across primates, “the bigger the neocortex of a primate, the bigger its social group.” Monkeys form alliances through grooming, rescue the friends they groom, and climb or fall in rank through those friendships. To play that game, you have to model what others know and want.

The classic test of that is the Sally-Ann test, where a child watches Ann move a marble while Sally is out of the room and has to say where Sally will look for it. Bennett’s claim is that theory of mind, learning by imitation, and planning for future needs are three uses of one new ability: a model of one’s own mind, which can then be pointed at others. Jane Goodall’s chimpanzees stripping twigs to fish for termites in Gombe, and the different techniques used by chimpanzees elsewhere, show skills that pass between individuals by watching. The AI parallels are some of the best in the book: ALVINN, the car Dean Pomerleau built at Carnegie Mellon in 1990, which learned to stay in its lane on a real highway by imitating human drivers, and the 2010 work by Pieter Abbeel, Adam Coates, and Andrew Ng, who used inverse reinforcement learning to teach a system to fly a remote-controlled helicopter by working out what the human pilot was trying to do.

The chapter title I will remember is “Why Rats Can’t Go Grocery Shopping”. In 2006 Miriam Naqshbandi and William Roberts offered squirrel monkeys dates and rats raisins, both treats that make them very thirsty, and a choice: a large helping with water only hours later, or a small one with water within half an hour. “Squirrel monkeys learn to select the low treat option, while rats continue to select the high treat option.” The rats, in Bennett’s words, “stuck with the flawed logic of ‘why give up extra raisins for water, I’m not even thirsty!’” Planning for a need you do not have yet is, for me, the clearest line between the assistants we build today and the ones we want. An agent that infers what you are trying to do, and what you will need next week, is doing what Bennett calls mentalizing. Most of ours still behave like the rats.

Speaking: tethering simulations together

The last part asks what makes humans different, and Bennett’s answer is careful. Chapter 19 walks through the attempts to teach apes language: Washoe, who saw a swan and signed “Water bird”, and Kanzi, who in Sue Savage-Rumbaugh’s test was given over six hundred commands in sentences he had never seen, such as “Go put some soap on Liz”, and carried them out more than 70 percent of the time, outperforming a two-year-old child. Bennett gives the critics their due (most of the apes were rewarded with treats, and rarely combined words into new phrases) and concludes that “The debate is not yet settled.” His position is that apes can learn a rudimentary language with great effort, but never pass a young child.

What humans have, he argues, is not a new language organ but a curriculum. Chapter 20 begins with Louis Victor Leborgne, who lost the ability to speak in 1830 and whose brain led Paul Broca to the language area that bears his name, and then turns to infants: proto-conversations, and joint attention, where a nine-month-old follows a mother’s gaze and checks that they both see the same thing. Chimpanzees do not do this. The AI parallel is Jeffrey Elman’s work in the 1990s on networks that predict the next word, which only learned complex sentences when he first showed them simple ones. “In other words, he designed a curriculum.”

Chapter 21 explains why language spread, and its answer is gossip. Dunbar eavesdropped on conversations and found that “as much as 70 percent of human conversation is gossip,” and Bennett argues that gossip plus the punishment of cheaters is what makes cooperation between strangers stable. With language, “the human hive mind emerged, creating an ephemeral medium for ideas to propagate and accumulate across generations.” The book’s definition of language is the one I took away from it: a way of tethering one person’s inner simulation to another’s. It also explains Bennett’s view of language models, which have the words without, as far as anyone can show, the simulation behind them.

The sixth breakthrough

Chapter 22, “ChatGPT and the Window into the Mind”, is the most honest chapter in the book. Bennett had written a set of questions to show that GPT-3 lacked common sense, because it predicts words without an inner simulation of the world: it did not know, for example, that looking up in a basement shows you a ceiling and not the sky. Then GPT-4 came out while the book was being finished, and “each question that I designed in this chapter to demonstrate a lack of common sense and physical intuition in GPT-3 was answered flawlessly by GPT-4.” He kept both in the book, and his conclusion holds up better for it. Without simulating and mentalizing, he argues, language models will miss something essential, and the humanlike AI we build one day will not be a language model: “language models will be merely a window to something richer that lies beneath.” I am less sure than he is that the window and the room stay separate, but it is the right question to ask of the systems I work with.

The conclusion is called “The Sixth Breakthrough”, and Bennett thinks it will be artificial superintelligence: intelligence moving from biology to silicon, no longer limited by the speed of neurons or the size of a skull. He ends on a question, “What should be humanity’s goals?”, which he says is a matter of values rather than truth. I agree, and few books on AI stop in a better place.

Where it dragged

The book is long, and it does not hurry. A great deal of it is behavioural studies: Thorndike’s cats, Pavlov’s dogs, rats in mazes, animals in front of mirrors, Jane Goodall’s chimpanzees and their tools. Each one is there for a reason and each one moves the argument forward; I would not cut any of them. But they are told at a steady, even pace, one experiment after the other, and few of them pulled me in the way the chapter on smell did. I found myself reading for the AI paragraph at the end of each chapter, and that is not the right way to read this book.

The other half is evolutionary biology, and here I part ways with the framing. Bennett tells every breakthrough as a story of deep time, pressure, and survival, and closes his chapter on simulation by saying that thinking was born “not within the clay creatures of Prometheus’s divine workshop” but in the tunnels and trees of a Jurassic Earth, which he calls “the real story.” I do not share that view, and I read the material the other way round, as I did with How Life Works: a layered design in which each layer builds on the one below is easier for me to see as engineered than as an accident that kept succeeding. That disagreement did not spoil the book, though, because its argument does not depend on it. The five breakthroughs work as a decomposition of intelligence whatever one believes about how they came to be, and that decomposition is the part I will keep.

Who should read it

Anyone who builds with AI and wants to know where the ideas came from and what is still missing. You do not need a background in neuroscience; Bennett explains everything from the ground up, which is part of why the book is long. Set aside time for it, read the five summaries first if you want the map before the territory, and expect to read it slowly, a part at a time.

I learned a lot from it. I was not prepared for its depth, and I think that showed in how slowly I read. I expect to come back to it, and I suspect a second reading, knowing where it is going, would earn it a higher score.

item.title: Win Everything, Control No One
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
The Infinity Machine opens with a scene that has nothing to do with Demis Hassabis. In 2015, after a talk at the Royal Society, Nick Bostrom asks Geoffrey Hinton why he keeps doing AI research if he thinks political systems will use it to terrorise people. Hinton answers that he could give the usual arguments, “but the truth is that the prospect of discovery is too sweet.” Mallaby says the story haunted him, and it sets the question for the whole book: if the people building this technology understand the danger, why do they build it anyway, and does it matter what kind of people they are?

His answer is a biography of Demis Hassabis, and it is also the best account I have read of how AI got from game-playing programs to where it is now. I give it 8.5 out of 10. It is required reading for anyone who wants to understand the people behind this technology, what drives them, and why nobody seems able to stop it.

What the book is

The book does two things. It tells a life: Hassabis watching his father play chess at four and beating adults within weeks, a chess master at thirteen, a game designer at Bullfrog before university, a failed games studio, a PhD in neuroscience, DeepMind, the sale to Google, AlphaGo, AlphaFold, the Nobel Prize, and the scramble after ChatGPT. And it tells the history of the field through its ideas, in the order they arrived. Mallaby had about thirty hours with Hassabis over three years and interviewed more than a hundred people around him, so the rivals and the people who fell out with him speak in their own words.

The title comes from Cambridge. Hassabis and his friend David Silver imagined a machine that would find the patterns in a near infinity of data, and Hassabis later recruited Mustafa Suleyman with the line that an infinity machine would have infinite potential (chapters 2 and 4). Behind the phrase is the problem of induction, which symbolic AI never solved and which the rest of the book watches deep learning and reinforcement learning solve, piece by piece.

A history of AI, told in the right order

Mallaby explains the technology twice, once with an analogy and once with the mechanism. For example:

  • How an image network learns (chapter 6). The first layers find edges and patches of colour, later layers find curves and textures, deeper ones find the outline of a paw, and the last ones name the cat. Then the mechanism: weights, biases, sixty million parameters nudged until inputs match outputs.
  • Why the Atari agent needed experience replay (chapter 6). An image classifier fed a sorted stack of photos, all cats first, concludes that everything is a cat. An agent stuck in one corner of a game has the same problem. Storing experiences and sampling them at random fixed it, and Hassabis saw in it what the hippocampus does during sleep.
  • Why the Atari agent needed a second network (chapter 6). An agent that keeps adding optimism to its own estimates is like a man who finds a couple of hundred-dollar bills on the pavement and concludes he will be a billionaire by walking for a month. Mallaby’s fix is a tennis coach who watches for a while before giving advice: one network plays with frozen weights, a second one learns, and the lessons are handed over only after a period of study.
  • AlphaGo as two kinds of thinking (chapter 9). A policy network proposes moves the way a strong player sees them at a glance, a value network judges positions, and tree search does the slow deliberate part, which Mallaby maps onto Kahneman’s System One and System Two.
  • Residual networks (chapter 12). Deep networks garble their signal like a game of telephone; skip connections are express lanes past the middle layers.
  • The transformer (chapter 12). Embeddings as a map of language with hundreds of dimensions, attention as knowing which earlier episode of a crime drama you need to understand this one, and a detour through Henri Bergson on time as attention rather than sequence.

The explanations need no background and do not talk down to the reader. The order matters as much: each chapter shows what the previous breakthrough made possible and what it could not do, so the chain from ImageNet to Atari to AlphaGo to AlphaZero to the transformer to AlphaFold to reasoning models reads as one argument. I drew that chain, with a source for every link, and the people who carried it from lab to lab, as two interactive figures in a companion note: Who contributed to AI.

The feud at the centre

The thread that ties the history together is the rivalry between reinforcement learning and deep learning. It starts as geography: Hinton’s deep learners in Toronto, Richard Sutton’s reinforcement learners in Alberta, barely speaking. The RL theorist Csaba Szepesvári admits that neural networks work in practice but he will not use them because he cannot prove anything about them; Hinton tells his student Vlad Mnih, who wants to combine the two, “I’ve tried that. It doesn’t work.” Mnih goes to London and does it anyway, and the Atari agent is the result (chapter 6).

From there the book shows the pendulum swinging, and it never lets either side win for long:

PeriodWho looked rightWhat happenedWhat the other side contributed
2006 to 2012Deep learningHinton’s deep belief networks, then graphics chips, then Alex Krizhevsky’s ImageNet win, trained in his bedroom; his three-person company sells to Google for $44 million (chapters 4 and 6)Nothing yet: the two camps barely talk
2013Both, for the first timeDeepMind’s Atari agent learns dozens of games from pixels and a score; the room at the NIPS conference goes silent at the Breakout tunnel (chapter 6)A convolutional network to see the screen, from deep learning; Q-learning, experience replay and a second network to keep its estimates honest, from RL
2014 to 2016Reinforcement learningAlphaGo beats Fan Hui five to nothing, then Lee Sedol four to one, with Move 37 (chapter 9)The policy and value networks that stand in for intuition are deep learning, trained first on 150,000 human games
2017Reinforcement learning, loudlyAlphaZero learns Go, chess and shogi from self-play alone, with no human games at all (chapter 12)A residual network from Microsoft, deep enough to fold AlphaGo’s two networks into one
2017 to 2019Deep learningLeCun calls RL the “cherry on the cake”; the transformer and GPT learn from unlabelled text, which removes RL’s two selling points, learning without human labels and generating its own data (chapter 12)Little, until post-training
2017 to 2020Neither aloneGaia, a simulated natural world for agents, fails; AlphaStar’s win rate against StarCraft II’s built-in bots jumps from 10 to 84 percent because of a transformer, then RL takes it to 99.8 percent against ranked humans; a pure self-play StarCraft agent never gets off the ground (chapter 13)Each needed the other, and neither could do it alone
2018 to 2020Deep learning, with biologyAlphaFold starts as an RL project and wins by mostly abandoning RL; “Protein folding is not a two-player game,” Hassabis says (chapter 15)A search step in the first AlphaFold, then nothing; the decisive ideas came from evolution and the transformer
2022 to 2023Deep learning, tamed by RLChatGPT and DeepMind’s unreleased Sparrow both become usable through reinforcement learning from human feedback; Silver’s attempt to bring machine RL to Gemini stalls, because nobody can write a reward for a good haiku (chapters 16 to 18)Human raters supply the reward that the game score used to supply
2024 onwardReinforcement learning againRewards from maths and logic problems with right answers teach models to reason step by step: OpenAI’s o1, Gemini Flash Thinking, DeepSeek’s R1-Zero; AlphaProof wins an Olympiad silver medal; Silver and Sutton announce the “Era of Experience” (chapters 19 and 20)The language models being trained are deep learning; RL now runs on top of them, and so does reward hacking

Every real breakthrough in the book combines both methods, and the side that looks wrong at any moment is usually waiting for the other side’s next advance.

What DeepMind got wrong

Mallaby is a sympathetic biographer, but he does not hide DeepMind’s mistakes. DeepMind’s 2010 business plan dismissed what it called the mistaken notion that language is intelligence expressed. Hassabis believed a model had to act in the world to understand it, and he misjudged GPT for years. He admits it: “you can’t be Nostradamus every time” (chapter 13).

Afterwards he explains why. He had assumed the space of human behaviour was nearly infinite; it turned out that the roughly fourteen trillion words on the internet capture most of it. He compares the internet to the coal and oil the Industrial Revolution happened to find in the ground: nobody built it for AI, and it did not have to be there. I made the same argument from the other side in my review of Tim Berners-Lee’s memoir, The Web Was the Training Set, and Hassabis reaches it from inside the lab.

The other mistakes were organisational. Google was stuck in Xerox PARC’s dilemma: it invented the transformer and could not ship a chatbot without endangering search. DeepMind was stuck in Bell Labs’ dilemma: a culture built for open-ended exploration could not switch to engineering when the path became obvious. DeepMind had a chatbot, Sparrow, with twenty-three behavioural rules and web search, nearly ready when ChatGPT launched, and it never shipped (chapters 16 and 17).

The people

Peter Thiel backed DeepMind because it seemed contrarian and cheap, never believed in it, and nearly let it run out of money (chapter 7). Elon Musk promised money, tried to buy DeepMind for Tesla or SpaceX in a phone call from a closet, then co-founded OpenAI against it after sitting on DeepMind’s own safety board (chapters 8 and 10). Mark Zuckerberg lost DeepMind at dinner when Hassabis noticed he was just as excited about virtual reality and 3D printing as about AI, then hired Yann LeCun to poach its staff (chapter 8). Larry Page called Musk a “speciesist” for preferring humans to machines (chapter 10). Sam Altman, seen mostly through the eyes of his rivals, appears as the man who wrote in 2015 that stopping humanity from developing AI was “almost definitely not” possible, and then did more than anyone to prove it. Dario Amodei turns up as the safety researcher who scaled GPT-2 and later left to found Anthropic.

Mustafa Suleyman’s story is the hardest to read. He was the friend of Hassabis’s younger brother and became a co-founder. His health work for the NHS was good (the Streams app cut the share of unnoticed urgent kidney cases from 12.4 to 3.3 percent, chapter 11) and was killed by a tabloid story about data. His campaign to put DeepMind under independent oversight ran for three years and failed (chapter 14). Then came a bullying investigation, a sabbatical, and a Bloomberg headline, and the friendship ended. Mallaby lets both men tell their side.

Why it cannot be governed

Coming out of the book, I am more convinced than before that AI cannot be stopped, and cannot be governed, at least for now. That is my conclusion, but the book supplies most of the evidence for it. Every attempt to govern it from inside the industry fails, and the governments arrive late, with voluntary commitments:

  • The ethics and safety board Google agreed to when it bought DeepMind met once, at SpaceX. Several of its guests then founded or funded a rival lab. “Our supposed advisers were really our rivals,” Hassabis says (chapter 10).
  • The independent panel that watched over DeepMind Health was shut down when Google absorbed the health team (chapter 14).
  • Project Mario, three years of negotiation for a DeepMind with a board of three Google directors, three DeepMind directors and three independents, ended with nothing. Reid Hoffman pledged a billion dollars to a DeepMind that walked away, and it never happened (chapter 14).
  • OpenAI’s nonprofit board fired Altman and lasted five days (chapter 18).
  • The pause letter in 2023 was signed by more than a thousand people, but not by the heads of the leading labs. Hassabis’s objection holds up: a moratorium on models while chips and data centres keep improving would hand the next race to whoever has the most compute when it ends (chapter 18).

By 2025 Hassabis has concluded that “Safety isn’t about governance structures” and that the best you can do is have a seat at the table. Mallaby calls this a “flimsy scaffolding of reassurance” and admits it may be the best on offer. I agree with him on both counts.

The parts I recognised

There is a line in chapter 3 about Hassabis’s “burning desire to play and win something, anything”, which his first games studio tried to satisfy with fantasy football and StarCraft. When a colleague finally beat him at table football, he declared that his soul was on fire. I laughed, because I recognise the feeling. I played in a chess club when I was young, StarCraft is still my favourite strategy game, and I follow the Korean Brood War scene closely enough to have built a site about it. So the chapters on AlphaStar, and on AlphaGo against Lee Sedol in front of two hundred million viewers in Korea, were personal in a way most AI history is not.

So were the games. I loved Peter Molyneux’s Black & White and later Fable, and Hassabis worked on the early design of Black & White because it was the first game whose creatures changed their own rules from the player’s slaps and strokes, a small reinforcement learning system in a commercial game (chapter 2). Before that, as a teenager, he built the simulated visitors of Theme Park, who got thirsty from salty chips and sick on roller coasters. The book draws a straight line from those simulated worlds to Gaia, DeepMind’s attempt at a simulated biosphere, and to Hassabis’s fascination with Conway’s Game of Life and emergence: put simple parts together and properties appear that none of the parts had. That is the question I keep coming back to in my own simulations, from Hotaru, a simulated neuron culture that learns to play Pong, to the engines in Kishi. Kishi plays chess, shogi and Go, the same three games AlphaZero learned, and the Learning to Play series is my small-scale version of the questions in chapters 9 and 12. Hassabis also reached the top of the English shogi rankings.

The future he wants is close to the one I want: biology solved by computation, robots and automation doing the work, and abundance. He grew up on Iain Banks’s Culture novels, and in chapter 7 he goes further than most people in the industry. He doubts universal basic income is the answer and prefers what he calls universal basic provision: housing, schooling, health care and travel at a level today’s millionaires enjoy, free to every citizen, with work for anyone who wants a Ferrari. Silver, at the end of chapter 20, proposes a human right to AI assistance. Neither is a plan, but both are better starting points than most of the policy debate.

Winning without controlling

Mallaby keeps two of Hassabis’s traits in view for the whole book, and they happen to be two I share. He is ferociously competitive: Hinton calls him the only person he has met who is more competitive than Hinton. And he insists, from chapter 2 onward, that he does not want to control anyone, saying it is “really bad to manipulate or control people”, a value he traces to his mother’s church. He also does not seem to care about money. At eighteen he refused to cash a £500,000 cheque from Molyneux so he could go to Cambridge. When he sold DeepMind, he and Suleyman negotiated the research budget before the price, and in the epilogue he says he would not have swapped the Nobel for any amount of money. He drives a ten-year-old Audi and his one luxury is a Liverpool season ticket.

Mallaby tests the claim about control, and the evidence is mixed:

  • At Elixir, Hassabis’s “Jedi mind trick” inspired a team past the point of honest feedback. “Who would’ve thought that you can actually inspire people too much?” he says later (chapter 3). A psychologist tells Mallaby that charismatic people cannot avoid dominating others, however hard they try.
  • He walked away from venture capital at Elixir because giving up half the company meant being controlled. At DeepMind he took nine times as many shares as his scientific co-founder because he wanted control of the mission (chapter 5).
  • He hated domination in both directions: he would not dominate, and he would not be dominated. When Suleyman challenged his direction, he let an investigation do what a conversation should have done (chapter 14).
  • In the epilogue Mallaby puts it to him directly: “He had told me repeatedly that he didn’t want to control others. And yet he did control people.” Hassabis answers that he exercises a reluctant power, because the things he wants to do require large teams.

For anyone who likes to win and dislikes power, this is a warning: the first trait puts you in situations where you have to exercise the power the second trait wants to avoid. Hassabis’s answer, that power is acceptable as a means to the work and never as an end, is the right one. But the book shows how much discipline it takes to keep it a means.

Where it falls short

The half point I hold back is mostly about distance. Mallaby states his verdict in the introduction, that Hassabis is “decent and public-spirited”, before the evidence, and although the book does test it, Hassabis gets the last word on most disputes. OpenAI and Anthropic are seen from outside, mostly through people who left them or competed with them, so Altman is drawn almost entirely by his rivals. And Mallaby editorialises in places where he could have reported: he is hard on the independent panel that criticised DeepMind Health, generous to DeepMind in the argument over Gemini’s benchmarks, and at one point says DeepSeek’s R1-Zero was, “for all intents and purposes”, self-aware, a claim the evidence he gives does not support.

The last chapters also read like dispatches. They race through benchmarks and product names that are already dated, and they lack the calm of the chapters about Cambridge, Elixir and AlphaGo. That may be unavoidable in a book finished in 2026 about a race still running, and none of it changes my recommendation.

Who should read it

Anyone who wants to understand the last fifteen years of AI through the people who made them, with the concepts explained along the way. No technical background is needed, and if you have one, the explanations are still worth reading for their order and their analogies. It pairs well with the forecasts on my reading log such as AI 2027: those describe where this might go, and this book shows who is driving and why, and how little anyone, including the drivers, controls the route.

The book ends with Hassabis in a pub, saying that it should feel amazing to watch his dreams come true and does not, because of the mad rush. He is still optimistic.

item.title: Learning to Play
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
This month I have been reading The Infinity Machine, Sebastian Mallaby’s biography of Demis Hassabis, the chess prodigy from North London who founded DeepMind, the laboratory behind AlphaGo and AlphaFold. I picked it up because I wanted to understand one of the early architects of the AI we now live with, told by someone who had thirty hours of his time, and because almost everything that interests me, games, simulations, the question of what a machine can learn on its own, runs through his story. A hundred pages in, there is a scene I have not been able to put down.

It is 1988 and Hassabis is twelve. He has bought a Commodore Amiga 500 with his chess winnings, and in Foyles, the big bookshop on Charing Cross Road, he finds a slim paperback: The Chess Computer Handbook by David Levy. He reads it in one sitting. Levy explains how a chess program is built from three parts. The board has to be turned into numbers. A function has to look at a position and say who is better. And a search has to try moves, and the replies to them, and the replies to those, cutting off the branches that are obviously bad because the tree grows faster than any computer can follow. Hassabis tries to build it, finds that the Amiga chokes on chess, and writes an Othello program instead, which beats his five-year-old brother.

I put the book down at that point, partly because I recognised the boy a little, and partly because I realised two things. The first is that those three parts are still the whole of a chess program. Thirty-eight years later, the strongest engines in the world are a board in numbers, an evaluation function, and a tree search with pruning; what has changed is that the evaluation function is now learned by a machine rather than written by a person, and that the machine learned it by playing against itself. The second is that the laptop on my desk has thirty thousand times the memory of that Amiga, and I had never built the three parts myself.

So I did, this month. I wrote three game engines in Rust, for chess, for Japanese shogi, and for Go, compiled them to WebAssembly so they play in a browser on my phone, and built the training loop that is supposed to make one of them stronger than I could make it by hand. The app is at kishi.raskell.io and the code is on GitHub. This is an account of why those three games, why those tools, and what happened when the ideas in the books met one ordinary machine.

The book, the man and the lab

Mallaby is not a technology writer by trade. He is a former contributing editor of the Financial Times, twice a Pulitzer finalist, now a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, and his earlier books were about money: hedge funds in More Money Than God, Alan Greenspan in The Man Who Knew, venture capital in The Power Law. That turns out to be the right background. The Infinity Machine is a biography and a company history at once, built on about thirty hours of conversation with Hassabis and more than a hundred interviews around him, and it takes the question of why someone would build a technology they believe to be dangerous as seriously as the question of how. It came out earlier this year. I am reading it slowly, and the AlphaGo chapters are still ahead of me, which I find I do not mind, because I would rather meet them with my own version of the thing running.

Hassabis, if you do not follow the field, is the person it now treats as its elder statesman, at fifty. Born in Finchley in 1976 to a Singaporean Chinese mother and a Greek Cypriot father, he was a chess master at thirteen and the second-strongest player of his age in the world. At sixteen he was co-writing Theme Park at the games studio Bullfrog, a game that sold millions. He read computer science at Cambridge, ran a games studio of his own for seven years, and then went back to university for a doctorate in neuroscience, because he thought the only way to build an intelligent machine was to understand the one existing example first. In 2010, in an attic on Russell Square, he founded DeepMind with Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman, at a time when almost nobody in the field believed that what they proposed was possible. The first real money came from a Peter Thiel fund whose partners rated the science A-plus and the business model an F.

DeepMind was conceived as a Manhattan Project for artificial intelligence, and its method is what connects the book to this article. The bet was to combine two branches of the field that were both unfashionable in 2010: deep learning, the layered neural networks Geoffrey Hinton had spent a quarter of a century defending, and reinforcement learning, in which a program learns from the consequences of its own actions rather than from labelled examples, with ideas from neuroscience on top. The proving ground was games, because games have rules you can write down and scores you can read off the board. The first result, shown in 2013, was one agent that learned to play Atari games from the pixels alone. Google bought the company in 2014. In 2016 AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol in Seoul, and in 2017 its successor, AlphaZero, learned chess, shogi and Go from nothing but the rules and games against itself, with one algorithm, and beat the strongest existing program at each. Those are the three games in this article, in that order, and self-play is the loop I built. AlphaFold followed in 2020, then the predicted shapes of two hundred million proteins, then the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2024. Even the name is a triple nod: to deep learning, to Deep Blue, and to Deep Thought, the computer in The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy that was asked for the answer to everything.

Why am I reading it? Partly for the obvious reason: I work on AI platforms for a living and wanted the story of one of the architects of this revolution from the inside, and the book is exactly that and more. Partly because of the parallels, which kept catching me off guard: a games designer who smuggled a simulation into a theme park, a competitor who cannot pass a board game without wanting to win it, a man who thinks of the world as information and of the mind as something that builds reality rather than records it. I recognise more of that than is comfortable. And partly because of the belief. Hassabis believed in artificial intelligence when almost nobody did, with a conviction the book is honest enough to call close to religious, and he was right. There is a strand of transhumanism running through the story, from the Iain Banks novels he read at Bullfrog to the Singularity Summit where DeepMind found its first investor, and he keeps a dry British distance from the Californian version of it. I have a strand of my own, with a different spin and from a different direction, and that is a subject for another piece. It is enough to say here that I did not come to the book as a sceptic.

What hooked me in those early pages, more than the prodigy story, is how often games are the way in. Hassabis learns programming through chess. His first intelligent program plays Othello. At Cambridge he learns Go from a professor and takes shogi far enough to reach the top of the English rankings. His friend David Silver, who will later lead the AlphaGo work, finds his way into the field through a textbook on reinforcement learning, read in the south of France after their games company failed. Mallaby traces the thread back to Claude Shannon’s 1950 paper on programming a computer to play chess, which Levy’s handbook had introduced to the twelve-year-old. Shannon wrote that chess programs had no practical importance, but that mastering a game might serve as “a wedge in attacking other problems of a similar nature and of greater significance”. That sentence is seventy-six years old and still the best one-line justification I know for spending a month on board games.

My own games

My own chess is a smaller story. I joined a chess club in my early teens, played the regional tournaments, and did well in a few of them: nothing that would have sent a chess columnist across the hall to talk to my father, as one did for Hassabis when he was six, and nothing I would put in the same paragraph as his career if the book had not put the two of us in the same bookshop. But the game stayed. I do not turn down a game when one is offered; the last one was against a coworker and friend on Union Square in San Francisco, this year. I have a weakness for the big outdoor sets with knee-high pieces, and there are two I like, one in Lucerne and one beside the Rhine here in Basel. On trains I play on lichess on my phone. And I have enjoyed, more than I expected to, the odd second life the game found in the 2020s, when a television series about a fictional prodigy sent people out to buy boards and grandmasters turned into streamers with audiences no tournament hall could hold. I did not see that coming, and I am not complaining.

The other half of my gaming life is what German calls Aufbauspiele, the building games: Anno, Die Siedler, the whole tycoon genre, anything where you lay down a world with rules and watch it run. Hassabis’s Theme Park is one of them, which made that chapter feel personal. The visitors who get thirsty when you oversalt the fries and buy more drinks, the riders who are sick when the coaster is too fast, are exactly the kind of mechanism I play these games for. I like games best when they try to mimic reality and let a thick ruleset generate stories nobody wrote, which is why I love Dwarf Fortress, and it is why I keep building simulations of my own, from a dish of neurons that learns under stimulation to a terrarium left to evolve. A chess engine, seen from that side, is the smallest simulation worth building: a complete world with rules, and inside it an agent that has to learn.

Why games, and why these three

Shannon’s point is practical. A game like chess has rules you can write down completely, a result you can read off the board without argument, and a depth that no amount of study has exhausted. That combination is rare. Most real problems have fuzzy rules, contested outcomes and no yardstick. A game gives you a laboratory where a new idea can be tested in an afternoon, against centuries of human knowledge, and the answer is a number.

Chess, shogi and Go also happen to be the three games along which the history of this field unfolded, in that order, and each one broke what had worked on the one before. That is why I picked all three rather than one.

Chess came out of northern India around the sixth century as chaturanga, travelled through Persia into Europe, and took its modern form, with the long-range queen and bishop, in Spain and Italy at the end of the fifteenth century. It is the game Shannon chose, the game Levy’s handbook teaches, and the one the classical method of search plus evaluation was built for. In 1997 IBM’s Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov by searching two hundred million positions a second on purpose-built chips, with an evaluation written and tuned by people. It was a triumph of the three parts and a disappointment to anyone hoping for insight: the machine won by looking further, not by understanding more. The interesting question, from Levy’s chapter onwards, was whether the evaluation function could be learned instead of written. For chess, that question was answered between 2018 and 2020 with a small neural network that lives inside the engine’s inner loop. It is called NNUE, and it was not invented for chess.

Shogi is the Japanese branch of the same family. It arrived in Japan by way of China and Southeast Asia by the eleventh century, took its present form by the sixteenth, and became an institution under the Tokugawa shoguns, who put the best players on stipends; the first Meijin, the title that still crowns a shogi champion, was awarded in 1612. Today it is played by millions in Japan, with a professional system, televised title matches, and a young star, Sota Fujii, who in 2023, at twenty-one, held all eight major titles at once. The board is nine by nine, each side has twenty pieces of eight kinds, and most of them promote when they reach the far third of the board. One rule makes it a different game. A captured piece changes sides, goes into the captor’s hand, and can later be dropped onto almost any empty square as a move. Nothing ever leaves the board for good, so the game never simplifies the way chess does. There are about eighty moves to choose from at a typical turn against chess’s thirty-five, the games are longer, and the endgame is a mutual race rather than a technical grind. For a programmer, drops make the evaluation function much harder to write by hand, which is why the learning happened here first. Computer shogi was transformed in 2006 by Bonanza, the first program whose evaluation was fitted to professional games rather than tuned by hand. In 2017 Ponanza beat the reigning Meijin, Amahiko Sato, and in 2018 Yu Nasu published the network design that Stockfish adopted for chess two years later. Shogi is where the idea I was chasing came from.

Go is older than both and simpler than either. It comes from China, where it is at least two and a half thousand years old and was counted among the four accomplishments of a cultivated person alongside music, calligraphy and painting; it reached Japan by the eighth century, where the Edo-period houses of professional players were funded by the shogunate, and it has deep roots in Korea, where it is called baduk. The rules fit on a card. Two players alternately place black and white stones on the intersections of a nineteen-by-nineteen grid. A group of stones with no empty points next to it is captured and removed. At the end, whoever surrounds more of the board wins, with a few points’ compensation to white for moving second. From those rules comes a game with around two hundred and fifty choices at every turn, games of two or three hundred moves, and positions that nobody has been able to score by hand. Levy’s three parts fail here. A search that looks four moves ahead in Go sees almost nothing, and there is no formula for who is winning to apply at the leaves. Go was the game that everyone in the field, including Hassabis, called the grand challenge, and it was the one DeepMind chose when it wanted to show what it had. The programs of the late 2000s had replaced the chess method with Monte Carlo tree search, which plays thousands of random games out to the end and counts who wins; that got to strong-amateur level and stuck. AlphaGo kept that search and gave it two neural networks, one to suggest moves and one to judge positions, trained first on human games and then on its own, and in March 2016 it beat Lee Sedol four games to one.

So: one game where the classical method works and the network replaces the evaluation; one where the same method strains and the network was invented; one where the method fails and the network has to guide the search itself. The three together are a short course in forty years of the field, and each one can be measured against opponents anyone can download.

Why I built it rather than read about it

Hassabis likes to cite Feynman’s line about not understanding what you cannot build, and it is the honest reason for this project. I have read the AlphaGo paper and the Stockfish NNUE write-ups more than once. I could explain the diagrams. I could not have told you what K is, or why a network that wins at equal search depth can lose at equal time, or how many hours of a laptop’s life a generation of self-play costs, because those are the things the papers leave out and the only way to learn them is to pay for them. Reading the book made the gap uncomfortable, and the same itch that makes me build terrariums wanted the world with the rules and the learner inside it running on my own machine.

The other reason is that the ingredients are, for the first time, all on my desk. The ideas are published and the reference implementations are open source. The laptop is a MacBook Pro with an Apple M4, ten cores and sixteen gigabytes of memory, which is not a research machine and has more general computing power than Deep Blue had. The browser on my phone can now run compiled code with vector instructions and real threads. And the writing of the code itself, which would have been a winter of evenings, took days with a coding agent, with me deciding what to build and the agent typing most of it. That belongs in the method: the agent wrote code, a match between two engines decided whether the code was any good, and the match does not care who wrote it.

Why Rust, and not PyTorch

The obvious way to do machine learning in 2026 is Python and PyTorch, and if the goal had been a model that answers questions on a server, that is what I would have used. The goal was an opponent on my phone, in a browser tab, offline, and that changed everything downstream.

A chess evaluation is called inside the search, about a million times a second, on one core, with no batching, rather than once per request. A network that lives there cannot be a model behind an API. It has to be a few hundred lines of arithmetic in the engine’s own language, run on integers, and updated incrementally as moves are made rather than recomputed from scratch, which is the whole trick of NNUE. The inference, in other words, had to be hand-written anyway. Once it was, the trainer was the same arithmetic run backwards, over a million parameters and inputs that are almost all zero, and it fitted in a few hundred lines too. Writing it is also how I found out what the framework would have hidden from me: the one constant I guessed instead of fitting turned a winning network into a losing one, and I would not have known why.

Rust is the language I write everything on this site in, from the neuron culture to the fantasy console, and it is the right tool for an engine for the usual reasons: no garbage collector in a loop that runs a million times a second, control over memory layout, and a compiler that produces WebAssembly with vector instructions from the same source as the native binary. One language runs from the self-play games on the laptop to the move on the phone, in one repository, and the web app has no build step. The trade-off is honest too. Training a small, sparse network on the CPU is fine. If the Go network ends up as a convolutional net with millions of dense parameters, Rust on ten cores will be slow, and I will have to decide whether to write a Metal kernel or admit that this is where the laptop study meets a GPU.

Why WebAssembly

Because the phone is the point. An opponent that lives on a server is not mine; an opponent in an app store is somebody else’s to approve. A web page that I add to my home screen, that works on a plane, and that runs the identical binary to the one on my laptop is the version I wanted, and in 2026 the browser can do it. WebAssembly has had 128-bit vector instructions for a while, and Safari now lets a page share memory between threads if it is served with the right isolation headers, so the chess engine on my phone searches on four cores. Lichess, the free chess site, runs Stockfish the same way for its analysis board, which was my proof that the approach was sound before I started.

The constraint also shaped the design more than any paper did. A network that has to be downloaded with the page and run on a phone has to be small; Kishi’s chess network is 820 kilobytes and is compiled into the engine binary. A search that has to run in a browser tab has to be frugal. Every decision that looks like taste in the code is really the phone saying no to something.

What happened

The chess engine came first: bitboards, a search with the usual family of pruning heuristics, and a hand-written evaluation borrowed from a well-known set of piece-square tables. Against Stockfish configured the way lichess configures its computer opponents, with twenty games a level on one core, it beats level 4 nineteen games to one, beats level 6 thirteen to seven, and loses to level 7 nineteen and a half to a half. If you have played the lichess computer, that places it: a solid club player, nowhere near the top.

Then the loop. The engine played itself from random openings for fifty-two minutes, which produced 5.6 million positions from fifty-seven thousand games, each labelled with what the search thought of it and how the game ended. A network trained on those positions in under twenty minutes beat the hand-written evaluation it replaced by 85 rating points, plus or minus 32, when both sides were allowed the same number of positions to look at. When both sides were allowed the same number of milliseconds, they came out even, because the network costs two and a half times as much per position. That is the whole problem of this kind of learning in one sentence, and I did not understand it before I had the numbers.

Shogi got its own engine with the same shape and a hand-written evaluation, which beats Fairy-Stockfish’s weakest setting twenty games to none and loses to a middling one eighteen to two. Go got the method of the late 2000s, Monte Carlo tree search with the shape patterns from the old MoGo program, and against GNU Go at its lowest level, with a second a move, it wins three games in ten. All three play on the phone. The chess one is the only one I would call a satisfying opponent at the top levels, and that is with the hand-written evaluation, because the trained network has not yet earned its place on the clock.

What this opened up

I started with one question, whether I could build Levy’s three parts, and I have ended the month with five better ones.

The chess network wins at equal search and draws at equal time. Does that change after more generations of self-play, as the games it learns from get stronger, or is a laptop-sized network always going to be paying for its own cost? The loop is running as I write this, at low priority, so the laptop stays usable. Why did one constant swing the result by 176 rating points, and what does that say about the contract between a learned component and the hand-tuned system it plugs into? Does the same loop work for shogi once the network can see where the kings are, which is what Nasu’s original design did and mine does not yet? Go needs the second kind of loop, where the search teaches the network which moves to look at, and I do not know what a laptop can train on a full nineteen-by-nineteen board; the AlphaGo chapters of the book, which I am about to reach, will tell me what it took in 2016, and I want to know what it takes in 2026 on a machine from a shop. And underneath all of it: how much of an engine’s strength survives the trip from a native binary to a browser tab on a phone, and what threads buy back.

Each of those is a few days of work and a few numbers, and I have started keeping a notebook in the repository so that the numbers are written down as they arrive, failures included. If the answers turn out to be as interesting as the questions, this may become the first of several pieces, one idea at a time, chess first, then shogi, then Go. Let’s see.

References

  • Sebastian Mallaby, The Infinity Machine: Demis Hassabis, DeepMind, and the Quest for Superintelligence (Penguin Press, 2026), chapters 1 to 5.
  • Claude Shannon, Programming a Computer for Playing Chess, Philosophical Magazine (1950).
  • David Levy, The Chess Computer Handbook (Batsford, 1984).
  • Yu Nasu, Efficiently Updatable Neural-Network-based Evaluation Functions for Computer Shogi (2018, in Japanese); Stockfish, Introducing NNUE Evaluation (2020).
  • David Silver and others, Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search, Nature (2016).
  • Kishi: the engines, the training loop, and the notebook of every run.
